state.target_passage:
The most promising candidates for room-temperature superconductors include several classes of materials that have shown intriguing properties, though none yet exhibit superconductivity at both ambient pressure and temperatures above 0 °C.

Hydrogen-rich hydrides are currently among the most exciting candidates. In these materials, such as lanthanum hydride (LaH10) under extreme pressure, superconductivity has been observed at temperatures as high as a few hundred Kelvin. However, these conditions require pressures of hundreds of gigapascals, far above ambient. Recent work has focused on stabilizing similar structures at lower pressures, with some theoretical and experimental hints suggesting that “near-ambient” pressures might be possible, but these findings are still controversial and not yet consistently replicated.

Certain hydrogen sulfide derivatives and other hydrides, like those incorporating sulfur or carbon (e.g., C₃N₄H or “cyanic hydride”-type structures), have also been theorized as potential room-temperature superconductors, but they are extremely unstable and difficult to synthesize in the necessary forms.

Transition metal oxides and doped cuprates have long been studied for high-temperature superconductivity, but even the best of these still require liquid nitrogen temperatures (around 77 K or -196 °C), not room temperature. Some recent theoretical proposals suggest that twisted multilayer graphene or other two-dimensional materials might harbor novel superconducting states at higher temperatures, particularly at specific magic angles or twist configurations, but experimental evidence so far indicates critical temperatures well below room temperature.

In the past few years, there have been several high-profile but unconfirmed reports of superconductivity at or above room temperature in materials like “redderite” (Ni₂ReO₆), certain carbonaceous sulfur hydrides, and metallic hydrogen synthesized in diamond anvil cells. However, in each case, subsequent attempts to reproduce the results have failed or led to revised interpretations,
